title: Cybersecurity · Episode 2
chapters: Backing up: never lose your photos again

units.t: Cybersecurity. Episode two.
In this episode: Backing up: never lose your photos again and Hacking: myth and reality.
Part one. Backing up: never lose your photos again.
In 1998, a single command wiped out most of Pixar's Toy Story 2.
What saved the film was a backup nobody knew existed.
Even experts lose data.
In 1998, while Pixar was making Toy Story 2, someone ran a command that began deleting the film's files from the shared drives.
Characters, sets and animation disappeared as staff watched.
The studio's regular backups turned out not to be working properly.
The film was rescued because technical director Galyn Susman, working from home after having a baby, had a fairly recent copy on her home computer.
It was carefully driven back to the studio and most of the work was restored.
Data vanishes in ordinary ways: a phone dropped in the surf, a stolen laptop, a drive that quietly fails, an accidental delete, a fire or flood.
Every drive eventually fails.
The question is not whether something will go wrong, but whether you will lose anything when it does.
The 3-2-1 rule.
A widely quoted rule of thumb, popularised by photographer Peter Krogh, is 3-2-1.
Keep at least three copies of anything important: the original plus two backups.
Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, such as your computer's internal drive and an external drive, so one type of failure cannot take them all.
Keep at least one copy offsite, somewhere physically separate, so a fire, flood or burglary at home leaves something behind.
Today that is usually a cloud backup service, but a drive kept at a relative's house or your workplace also counts.
The rule is not magic, but it makes you think about every way your data could be destroyed at once.
A copy out of reach.
Many people assume their files are safe in iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox.
Most of these are built mainly to sync, keeping files identical across devices.
So a deleted folder or overwritten document can spread to every device within seconds.
Many keep deleted files and older versions for a limited time, so learn how long and how to restore them.
Ransomware is software that encrypts your files and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the key.
Paying guarantees nothing and funds criminals.
A drive that is permanently plugged in can be encrypted too.
Keep a backup drive unplugged except during backups, or use a cloud service that keeps older versions.
The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists regular backups among its essential strategies.
Phones and photos.
For many people the irreplaceable files are photos and videos of children, travels and people who are no longer here.
Most now live on a phone, which is easy to lose, drop or break.
iPhones and Android phones can both back up automatically to the cloud, but the free storage is often small.
Once it fills up, backups can silently stop.
Check your phone's settings to see when it last backed up successfully.
Paying a few dollars a month for more storage is cheap insurance.
Every so often, download your photo library to a computer or external drive as well, so your memories do not depend on a single company or account login.
Test it, then automate it.
Pixar's backups were running, or so everyone thought, until the day they were needed.
Every few months, pick a random file or photo and try to recover it from each backup.
Check that it opens.
Make sure you know your cloud password and have two-factor authentication sorted, or your backup may be locked behind a login you cannot remember on the day your phone is lost.
Nobody remembers to copy files by hand every week, so automate.
Turn on automatic phone backups, use Time Machine on a Mac or File History on Windows with an external drive, and add a cloud service for the offsite copy.
Start with photos, important documents and tax records.
Any backup is infinitely better than none.
The key idea: Data is lost through ordinary accidents and failures, even at world-class studios, so it can happen to you.
Part two. Hacking: myth and reality.
Forget the hoodie in a dark room typing green code.
Real hacking is often slower, stranger and much more human than the movies suggest.
Hackers and their hats.
The word 'hacker' began as praise.
In the late 1950s and 1960s, members of a model railway club at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology used 'hack' for a clever, playful technical solution.
Only in the 1980s, as computers spread and break-ins made headlines, did it come to mean someone who enters systems without permission.
Security people now borrow hat colours from old Western films.
White hats test systems with permission and help fix weaknesses; many are penetration testers, paid to attack an organisation's defences before criminals do.
Black hats break in illegally for money, data, disruption or bragging rights.
Grey hats probe without permission but report the flaw rather than exploit it.
Even then, unauthorised access to a computer is a crime in Australia under Commonwealth and state laws.
Easy doors, many attackers.
Real attacks are rarely feats of genius.
Criminals use automated tools to scan the internet for computers running outdated software with publicly known flaws, then exploit the ones that haven't been patched.
Others use leaked passwords, cloud storage left open to the world, or accounts without multi-factor authentication.
A 'zero-day' is a flaw the software maker doesn't know about, so no fix exists.
These are rare and valuable, and mostly used by well-resourced groups, including some linked to governments.
Attackers range from opportunists with ready-made tools, to organised gangs, to state-linked groups pursuing espionage or disruption, to hacktivists with political aims.
The Australian Signals Directorate defends against serious cyber threats and publishes an annual cyber threat report.
Hacking people.
Often the easiest way into a system is through a person.
Social engineering means manipulating people into handing over access or information.
Examples include a phishing email, a phone call pretending to be IT support, a fake courier who tailgates staff through a secure door, or a USB stick left in a car park labelled 'salaries'.
The American hacker Kevin Mitnick, once among the FBI's most wanted, became famous for talking his way into systems rather than cracking code.
He later worked as a security consultant.
Technology can't fully fix this problem, which is why training people to pause and verify matters so much.
The ransomware threat.
Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts an organisation's files, then demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the key.
Many gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it, called double extortion.
Some operate like businesses, with specialists, customer support for paying victims, and affiliates who rent their ransomware.
In 2017 the WannaCry attack spread worldwide within days and disrupted parts of Britain's National Health Service.
Hospitals, councils, schools and businesses of all sizes are targets.
Paying guarantees nothing and funds further crime, so governments generally advise against it.
Since 2025, many Australian businesses must report ransom payments to the government.
Offline backups are the best defence.
Defenders and bounties.
The good news is that most attacks target easy weaknesses, so basic hygiene defeats many of them.
Keep devices and apps updated, use unique passwords or passkeys, turn on multi-factor authentication, and keep a backup that isn't permanently connected.
Be sceptical of unexpected messages and verify requests independently.
Companies also invite hackers to help.
Bug bounty programs reward anyone who finds a security flaw and reports it privately, so it can be fixed before criminals find it.
Netscape ran one of the first in 1995, and payouts for serious flaws can now reach tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars.
If hacking fascinates you, learn legally through capture-the-flag competitions, practice labs and TAFE or university courses.
The key idea: The word 'hacker' began as praise for clever tinkering, and hat colours now separate permission from crime.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the Toy Story 2 story show about backups?
Answer. Even top studios can nearly lose everything.
Question two. What makes a hacker a 'white hat'?
Answer. They test systems with permission.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
